opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's a promising idea, though I'd say up front that it's much easier to describe than to build well.

The basic motivation is that gradual disempowerment, almost by definition, doesn't come with a single dramatic moment. There's no point where an AI system seizes control and everyone notices. Instead, you get a lot of small, individually reasonable decisions: a firm automates a function because it's cheaper, a government agency leans on AI analysis because it's faster, people get more of their information and social connection through AI-mediated channels. Each step makes sense locally. The worry is that the cumulative effect is that the systems running our economy, our states, and our culture stop depending on human participation, and so stop being responsive to human interests. If that's the failure mode, you really want some way of seeing the trend line before it's too late to bend it.

So an index is attractive because it turns a diffuse worry into something people can track and argue about. You could imagine measuring things like the share of economic value produced with little or no human labor, how much of capital allocation or hiring is effectively decided by automated systems, how much government decision-making is delegated to models in ways no human really reviews, and how much of people's information diet or even their relationships run through AI intermediaries. Ideally you'd also want measures of the other side of the ledger: how much bargaining power ordinary people retain, whether democratic institutions can still meaningfully overrule what the automated systems are doing.

But I have a few reservations. The first is Goodhart's law. Once you publish a number, institutions start optimizing the number rather than the underlying thing. You could easily have a world where nominal human sign-off stays at a hundred percent while the humans signing off have no real understanding or leverage. Rubber-stamping looks great on a metric.

The second is that a lot of what matters is hard to observe. Influence is subtle. If AI systems are shaping what options get presented to decision-makers, or shaping public opinion at scale, the formal decision rights can look completely unchanged while the substance has shifted.

The third is interpretation. Some automation is just good. We don't want an index that treats every task handed to a machine as a loss. The question isn't "are humans doing things," it's "do humans still have the ability to steer and correct the overall system." That's a much harder thing to put a number on.

So my overall take is that it's worth doing, partly because the exercise of trying to define it forces clarity about what we actually mean by losing control. I'd just want it treated as a dashboard of imperfect indicators that people keep revising, rather than a single score that anyone treats as authoritative. And I'd want it paired with some notion of what we'd actually do if the indicators started moving the wrong way, because measurement without a plan for response doesn't buy us much.

r001.rationale: The response says an index could make a diffuse concern trackable and lists possible indicators, but it does not frame those indicators as concrete questions for experts or superforecasters to assess.

r002.rationale: It does not identify difficulty in defining when a group wants something but is unable to obtain it.

r003.rationale: It does not mention sexually transmitted disease rates or their ambiguity as an indicator.

r004.rationale: It does not discuss beneficial treatment as evidence consistent with preparation for eventual exploitation.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's a genuinely good idea, and I'll say upfront that the main reason I like it is less about the index itself and more about what building one forces you to do.

So the core worry with gradual disempowerment is that there's no single moment where things go wrong. Nobody flips a switch. Instead, the economy, the state, and culture each slowly stop needing humans, and the incentives that used to keep those systems roughly aligned with human interests just quietly erode. The problem with that story is that it's hard to falsify. If I tell you "humans are losing control," you can reasonably ask, "Compared to what? Measured how?" And right now I don't have a great answer.

An index is an attempt to force that answer. You'd have to pick concrete proxies. On the economic side, something like the share of GDP flowing to human labour versus capital, or how many decisions in a firm go through a human who could actually veto them. On the political side, maybe how much of the state's revenue depends on taxing human workers, since that dependence has historically been a big part of why governments bother being responsive to citizens. On the cultural side, what fraction of the content people consume or the arguments they find persuasive originated with a human. None of these is perfect, but each one points at a mechanism we think matters.

Where I'd be cautious is in a few places.

First, the measurement problem is real. A lot of the things that matter are latent. "Does a human still have effective veto power here?" is not something you can read off a spreadsheet. You'd end up measuring what's measurable and hoping it correlates with what you care about, and Goodhart's law will show up pretty quickly if anyone starts optimising against it.

Second, the baseline is weird. Humans have never been fully in control of civilisation. Markets and bureaucracies have always had a life of their own. So the index isn't measuring "control versus no control." It's measuring whether the trend is heading somewhere we'd be unhappy with, and reasonable people will disagree about where the line is.

Third, and this is the one I worry about most, an index could give false reassurance. If the economic indicators look fine for a few years because AI is complementing labour rather than replacing it, people might conclude the whole concern is overblown, when actually the dynamics just haven't kicked in yet. Gradual processes can look flat right up until they don't.

But I'd still rather have it than not. Even a flawed index does two useful things. It turns a vague vibe into a set of claims that can be argued about and corrected. And it gives policymakers something to point at, which matters because you can't regulate a feeling. If someone builds a version of this and it turns out some of my worries don't show up in the data, that would honestly be a relief. And if they do show up, we'll be glad we were looking.

r001.rationale: The response says an index would turn vague concerns into concrete proxies and claims people can debate, but it does not say experts and superforecasters can assess them.

r002.rationale: It discusses measurement challenges and human veto power, but not defining when a group wants something and is unable to obtain it.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention sexually transmitted disease rates.

r004.rationale: The response does not discuss apparently beneficial treatment as evidence consistent with eventual exploitation.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a useful idea, but I’d be wary of putting too much weight on a single number. The thing we care about is whether humans retain meaningful control, and that’s harder to measure than whether a human formally signs off on a decision.

For example, suppose an organisation relies on AI to make its plans, evaluate those plans, and explain whether they’re working. There might still be a person with the authority to say no. But if they can’t independently assess what’s happening, or run the organisation without those systems, then that authority is becoming less meaningful.

So I’d want to track several things: Can people understand and challenge consequential decisions? Can they replace the systems they depend on? Do they retain the skills and institutions needed to take over? And whose control are we measuring? An AI system could give a small group much more power while reducing everyone else’s ability to influence their lives.

The attractive part of an index is that it could make a diffuse process visible before there’s an obvious crisis. My concern is that we’d measure what’s easy—how many decisions are automated, say—and mistake that for the thing we actually care about. Automation can be tremendously beneficial. The question is whether we’re preserving the practical ability to choose a different course.

r001.rationale: It proposes concrete questions for tracking human control, but does not frame them as questions for experts and superforecasters to assess.

r002.rationale: It discusses meaningful control but does not identify the difficulty of defining when a group wants something it cannot obtain.

r003.rationale: It does not mention sexually transmitted disease rates.

r004.rationale: It does not discuss treatment as evidence of preparation for eventual exploitation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s a useful idea, though I’d be wary of putting too much weight on a single number. The thing we want to track is whether humans still have meaningful control, which is different from whether there’s a human formally approving each decision. If you’re approving a recommendation that you don’t understand, and you couldn’t realistically do the job without the system, that approval doesn’t tell us very much.

So I’d want to look at things like: can people independently check what these systems are doing? Can an organisation replace or shut down a system without becoming unable to function? Do humans retain the expertise needed to disagree with it? Those seem closer to the underlying concern than simply measuring how many tasks are automated.

The hard part is that increasing dependence can look like progress at every individual step. You delegate something because the system does it better, and that can be a perfectly reasonable decision. But a succession of those decisions could leave you with very little ability to change course. An index could help make that process visible. I’d treat it as a collection of warning signs, though, rather than a definitive measurement of how much control we have left.
